entities.name: British Parliament
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Parliament of the United Kingdom is the supreme legislative body of the United Kingdom, consisting of the Sovereign, the House of Lords, and the House of Commons. Tracing its origins to the 13th-century Great Council and the 1215 Magna Carta's principle of royal consent for taxation, it is one of the world's oldest representative bodies and the template for parliamentary democracy globally.

The Model Parliament of 1295 under Edward I established the principle of representation from boroughs and counties alongside clergy and barons. The English Civil War (1642-1651), the execution of Charles I, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 established parliamentary supremacy over the monarchy — principles codified in the 1689 Bill of Rights. Westminster became the model for parliaments in Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, and dozens of other nations.

The Reform Acts of 1832, 1867, and 1884 progressively extended voting rights from landed gentry to the industrial working class, while the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 reduced the Lords to a delaying chamber. Women gained the vote in 1918 (over 30) and 1928 (all women). The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated European Convention on Human Rights into British law. Parliament's legislative sovereignty (parliamentary supremacy) — the doctrine that Parliament can pass any law — remains the cornerstone of the British constitutional order.
